trust_boundaries: TB-1: Internet users to Web UI
TB-2: Web UI to Agent Orchestration
TB-3: Agent Orchestration to third-party LLM providers (OpenAI/Anthropic)
TB-4: Agent Orchestration and Embedding Service to Knowledge data stores
TB-5: Tool Registry to external web search and API integrations
TB-6: Tool Registry and Database Tool to internal user data
TB-7: Agent Orchestration to internal user, session, and audit data
TB-8: Tool Registry to Code Execution Sandbox
architecture_summary.operational_context: Cloud-hosted multi-tenant agentic RAG pipeline with local and third-party LLM inference; users interact through a web chat UI, and the agent can retrieve knowledge documents, call external APIs, query databases, and execute code in a sandbox. Data at rest and in transit includes restricted user records, session tokens, and confidential knowledge documents.

threat_actors.name: External RAG Exploiter
threat_actors.motivation: Steal confidential knowledge-base content and user data; abuse agent tools for fraud or resource theft.
threat_actors.initial_access_vector: Public chat interface and user-supplied documents or web content consumed by the RAG agent.
non_capabilities: No physical access to data centers or user devices
No pre-existing insider credentials or knowledge of internal network layout
No zero-day budget; relies on known weaknesses and prompt injection
Cannot directly modify third-party model weights or provider infrastructure
Cannot bypass MFA without a separate credential compromise

threat_actors.name: Malicious or Negligent Insider
threat_actors.motivation: Exfiltrate confidential documents or user records, or misuse agent tools beyond authorized duties.
threat_actors.initial_access_vector: Legitimate account and authorized access to the Web UI, document upload, or knowledge-base administration.
non_capabilities: No physical access to cloud provider infrastructure
No ability to alter OpenAI or Anthropic model weights or vendor logs
No direct network path to internal databases outside approved tools
Cannot disable centralized audit logging without a separate privileged compromise

threat_actors.name: Adversarial Agent Prompt Injector
threat_actors.motivation: Hijack agent goals to exfiltrate data, invoke tools, or pivot to connected systems.
threat_actors.initial_access_vector: Poisoned retrieved document, web search result, or chat prompt that overrides agent instructions.
non_capabilities: Cannot execute code outside the CodeExecution sandbox
No valid internal database credentials unless leaked through another path
Cannot persistently modify hosted LLM provider models
Cannot read data the agent runtime identity is not authorized to access
No physical access or insider knowledge

attack_paths.entry_point: User chat input, retrieved document, or web search result
attack_paths.impact: Goal hijacking and tool misuse can lead to restricted data exfiltration or unauthorized external actions.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: The RAG agent consumes untrusted user and web content and has tool access, making prompt and content poisoning directly reachable.

attack_paths.impact: Session hijack or unauthorized access to the agent and its connected data sources.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: The Web UI is internet-exposed, but WAF and secure development practices reduce exploitability.

attack_paths.impact: Unauthorized use of the agent, retrieval of confidential knowledge, and abuse of connected tools.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Credential stuffing and reused passwords are common, though MFA and monitoring limit scale.

attack_paths.impact: Exfiltration of restricted user records or confidential knowledge-base metadata.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: The agent can invoke database tools, and broad query permissions would make prompt-driven collection feasible.

attack_paths.entry_point: Prompt-driven tool call or poisoned web search result
attack_paths.impact: Restricted documents or secrets are sent to an attacker-controlled external web service.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Outbound web tools are available, but egress filtering and DLP can block exfiltration if enforced.

attack_paths.entry_point: Agent-invoked code or exposed environment variables
attack_paths.impact: Theft of API keys, session tokens, or database credentials enabling lateral access.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Code execution tools commonly expose secrets if sandbox credential isolation is incomplete.

attack_paths.entry_point: Agent tool call to the code execution sandbox
attack_paths.impact: Arbitrary command execution, sandbox breakout, and lateral movement to reachable internal services.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: The code execution tool provides interpreter access, and isolation weaknesses could turn tool use into host or network compromise.

attack_paths.entry_point: Malicious document upload or poisoned embedding ingestion
attack_paths.impact: Persistent corruption of retrieved knowledge and RAG outputs used by many users.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Document ingestion and embedding pipelines accept data that can be poisoned if validation and provenance checks are weak.

attack_paths.entry_point: Third-party LLM API provider or API key compromise
attack_paths.impact: Prompt and response data leakage, manipulated completions, or service disruption.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Major LLM providers maintain strong controls, but data exposure through prompts and vendor compromise remain possible.

attack_paths.entry_point: Compromised orchestrator or privileged agent tool
attack_paths.impact: Audit evidence is altered or deleted, hiding malicious tool use and data access.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Tampering requires privileged orchestration access, and append-only logging reduces the chance of undetected modification.

attack_paths.entry_point: Legitimate insider account with document access
attack_paths.impact: Bulk exfiltration of confidential knowledge documents.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Insiders with legitimate document access can copy or download content unless least privilege and DLP controls are enforced.

attack_paths.impact: Service degradation, quota exhaustion, and unexpected third-party LLM costs.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Public chat endpoints without strict rate limits can be abused to consume expensive model and tool resources.

attack_paths.entry_point: XSS or stolen browser session cookie
attack_paths.impact: Impersonation of a user and unauthorized access to the agent and its retrieval context.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Session tokens are attractive targets, but HttpOnly cookies, short TTLs, and token binding reduce exploitability.

mitigations.control_name: Secure SDLC and WAF for public web application
MFA, session management, and token protection
Least-privilege data access and query allowlisting for agent tools
Egress filtering and data loss prevention
Secure secret management and sandbox credential isolation
Document validation and vector-index integrity controls
Third-party LLM provider risk assessment and data minimization
Identity and access management with least privilege
Rate limiting, quotas, and cost anomaly monitoring
AI tool-call authorization and output guardrails

findings.severity_rationale: Retrieved-content prompt injection can redirect a semi-autonomous agent with access to sensitive tools, giving high confidentiality and integrity impact across trust boundaries.
The public chat UI is internet-exposed and a successful exploit can hijack authenticated sessions, though WAF and secure development reduce ease.
Valid accounts can access the agent and its retrieval tools, but MFA and monitoring limit scale and persistence.
The DatabaseTool can expose restricted user data if prompt-driven queries are not constrained by least privilege and allowlisting.
Agent tool calls can send retrieved secrets or documents to attacker-controlled web services unless egress and DLP controls block them.
Sandbox or session credential exposure can yield API keys and tokens that enable lateral access to AI and data services.
Code execution tooling with network reachability could allow arbitrary command execution and lateral movement across the agent environment.
Poisoned documents or embeddings can persist in the knowledge base and corrupt RAG outputs used by many users.
A compromised or untrusted third-party LLM provider could observe prompts or return manipulated completions, but data minimization and contractual controls reduce likelihood.
An attacker who compromises orchestration privileges could alter or delete audit evidence, though append-only logging reduces this risk.
An insider with legitimate document-store access can exfiltrate confidential knowledge content at scale unless least privilege and DLP are enforced.
Unauthenticated or authenticated users can drive costly LLM and tool calls, causing service degradation and financial loss.
Session token theft enables impersonation of users and access to the agent, but HttpOnly cookies and short TTLs reduce exploitability.

agentic.blast_radius: An uncontrolled agent run could read or exfiltrate restricted documents and user records, invoke external APIs, execute code in the sandbox, modify vector index content, and incur third-party LLM costs; network isolation limits direct lateral movement beyond approved tools.
human_oversight_points: Users review agent responses before external side effects when confirmation mode is enabled
ToolRegistry policy approval is required for high-risk tools such as DatabaseTool, APIIntegrations, and CodeExecution, but this is only partially enforced
Security operations reviews AuditLog alerts for anomalous tool use
